author: reek
body: The verb is the point. FactSync could already reconcile two stores, but a sync offer publishes your whole store to ask a question and the reply serves the answerer's whole store back. This asks for one hash.

author: reek
body: A LYING PEER IS CAUGHT BY ARITHMETIC, NOT BY TRUST. accept-reply hashes the work that came back and refuses it unless it addresses the hash that was asked for. Three ways to lie are tried: send a different work, forge content under the asked-for hash, and answer a question nobody asked. All three are refused, and none of the refusals needs to know anything about the peer. This is what lets the transport be untrusted.

author: reek
body: The fourth case is a correction, and it is worth keeping. Appending bytes to the reply is NOT corruption and is NOT refused: the work's content is length-prefixed on the wire, so a decoder takes exactly the bytes the length names and trailing garbage never reaches the work. A first cut of this test called that a corrupted work and expected a refusal; the code was right and the test was wrong. Corrupting a work means changing the content the hash addresses, which is what the forgery case does.

author: reek
body: A miss is empty, not an error. A peer that does not hold a work is ordinary.

author: reek
body: And the wire round-trips: the request and the reply survive encode/decode through the same framing every other agent message uses, because a verb that only works in-process is not a verb.

author: reek
body: The wire, both ways: encode the message to a tag and a body, then decode it back. Anything that survives this is a real message and not a record that happens to be in scope.

author: reek
body: The work is split across functions rather than one long chain of lets. A first cut put all of it in `opening` -- twenty-one bindings deep -- and the COMPILER crashed on it (`!EXC=54`, a wild read). The Developer's Guide warns that twenty or more chained lets nest the scope too deep; that is not a style note.
